passage: Payal waited outside the school counsellor's room, reading Kunal's last message again: "Did I do something?" Two weeks ago they'd spent every free period together, planning the science fair. Then, the night he said, "You're my closest friend," she blocked him. She didn't know why, only that her chest had gone tight and she'd wanted to run. It had happened before, with a girl in class eight. Inside, Mrs Rao listened without interrupting. "Wanting people near and then needing to escape is exhausting," she said. "We can work on this together, weekly. With your parents' okay, I'd also like you to meet our visiting psychologist." Payal nodded, then unblocked Kunal and typed, "Not you. Me. I'll explain soon."

qa.q: What did Kunal's last message say?
qa.a: It said, "Did I do something?"

qa.q: What did Payal feel the night Kunal called her his closest friend?
qa.a: Her chest went tight and she wanted to run, a fear that came just as the friendship got close.

qa.q: What turning point happened in the counsellor's room?
qa.a: Mrs Rao offered weekly sessions and a visiting psychologist, Payal agreed, and then unblocked Kunal to tell him it wasn't his fault.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt after being suddenly blocked?
qa.a: He was likely confused and hurt, wondering what he had done wrong.

grounding: A teenager who cut off a close friend just as they grew closer starts regular help from a school counsellor and a psychologist.

passage:
Ojas,
I owe you more than the three words I sent last month ("Leave me alone").
You were the best friend I'd had in years. We talked every night. Then you invited me to your cousin's wedding, to meet your whole family, and something in me panicked. I picked a stupid fight about cricket and walked out. I've done this before. Get really close, then burn it down before anyone can leave me first.
My khala noticed I'd stopped coming out of my room and took me to see a counsellor. I go every Tuesday now. It's slow, but I'm starting to understand the pattern.
I'm not asking you to forget it. I'm saying sorry, and that it was never about you.
Farhan

qa.q: Where had Ojas invited Farhan?
qa.a: Ojas invited Farhan to a cousin's wedding, to meet the whole family.

qa.q: What was Farhan afraid of when the friendship got very close?
qa.a: Farhan was afraid of being left, so ending things first felt safer.

qa.q: What turning point is helping Farhan change?
qa.a: Farhan's khala noticed and took Farhan to a counsellor, and the weekly sessions are helping Farhan understand the pattern.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading that it was never about Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas may feel relieved to know the fight wasn't caused by anything Ojas did, though still hurt by it.

grounding: A teenager writes to a friend about craving closeness, then wrecking it, and about starting weekly sessions with a counsellor.

passage: You know what I did to Abhinav? For three months he was my whole world. We talked every night; I told him things I'd never told anyone, about when my mother left. Then one day he said, "I'm really glad I know you," and I felt this cold panic, like the floor had opened. So I blocked him. Everywhere. No reason. I'm Ayesha, sixteen, and I've done it to three friends now. Last month the school counsellor said something that stuck: "Maybe getting close feels like waiting to be left, so you leave first." I cried in her office. I see her every Tuesday now. Last week I unblocked Abhinav and sent one line: "It wasn't you. I'm working on it."

qa.q: On which day does Ayesha see the counsellor?
qa.a: Every Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when Abhinav said he was glad to know Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha felt a cold panic, as if closeness meant being left, and blocked him.

qa.q: What turning step helped Ayesha, and why?
qa.a: Seeing the school counsellor every week, because it helps Ayesha understand the fear behind leaving first.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel receiving "It wasn't you"?
qa.a: Abhinav might feel relieved and less confused, after being blocked with no reason.

grounding: Shows a teen who craves closeness then cuts a friend off, linked to early loss, and gets help from a trusted counsellor.

passage:
July: Nilesh and Himani became inseparable in the new Class 11 section: tiffins, bus rides, late-night voice notes. He told her things about the year his father spent in hospital that he'd told no one.
August, a Monday: Himani laughed with someone else in the corridor. Nilesh stopped replying, sat at the other end of the bus and told everyone she was fake.
September, a Friday: His mother found him awake late, saying he wrecked every friendship. She sat with him till he slept, and the next day took him to the school counsellor, where he began weekly sessions. He sent Himani a note: "You didn't deserve that."

qa.q: What did Nilesh tell others about Himani in August?
qa.a: That she was fake.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when Himani laughed with someone else?
qa.a: He likely felt afraid of losing her and hurt, so he pushed her away first.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh begin to change?
qa.a: His mother's calm support and weekly sessions with the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Himani feel reading the note?
qa.a: Himani may feel hurt but also relieved and respected, since he admits she did nothing wrong.

grounding: Shows a teen swinging from an intense bond to cutting a friend off, linked to early fear, and starting professional help.

passage: You think your Raghav-chacha was always this calm? Sit, I'll tell you. After your Dada died, Raghav was fifteen, and he fell into friendships the way a boy falls into a well: one best friend, day and night, until suddenly he'd pick a fight and never speak to him again. Three friends that way in one year. Poor Mohan cried at our gate. I scolded Raghav at first; that only made him slam doors. Then the headmaster suggested a counsellor in town. I, Gargi, who thought such things were for other families, took him every Saturday on the bus for two years. Slowly he learned closeness wasn't a trap. Mohan is still his friend. He came to your naming ceremony.

qa.q: Who cried at their gate?
qa.a: Poor Mohan.

qa.q: What might Raghav have been feeling when he cut friends off?
qa.a: He was likely afraid of losing people again after his father died, so closeness felt dangerous.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Gargi stopped scolding and took Raghav to a counsellor every Saturday for two years.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt when Raghav stopped speaking to him?
qa.a: Mohan was hurt and confused, crying at the gate after losing a close friend with no reason.

grounding: Shows a teen, after a loss, swinging between intense friendships and cutting people off, helped by a counsellor.

passage:
The storm had knocked out the power on the night before the maths exam, and Sumit sat on the stairs with his phone at nine per cent.
Last month he and Zainab had been inseparable: studying together, eating every lunch together. Then, a week ago, he had stopped replying and told a friend she was "too much". Now he stared at her last message: "Did I do something?"
He wanted to type, "No, I miss you." His thumb hovered. He was afraid she'd leave first, the way his mother had left when he was six.
Tomorrow was his session with Ms Kapoor, the counsellor he had been seeing since spring. She had said, "Notice the moment you want to cut someone off."
This was that moment. With one per cent left, he typed, "You didn't. I got scared. Can we talk after the exam?" The screen went black.

qa.q: What did Sumit tell a friend about Zainab?
qa.a: He said she was "too much".

qa.q: Why did Sumit hesitate before replying to Zainab?
qa.a: He missed her but was afraid she would leave first, the way his mother had left when he was six.

qa.q: How did the counsellor's advice help Sumit in this moment?
qa.a: Ms Kapoor had told him to notice when he wants to cut someone off, so he recognised the moment and sent an honest reply instead of staying silent.

qa.q: What might Zainab feel reading "I got scared" after a week of silence?
qa.a: Zainab might feel relieved it wasn't something she did, yet still hurt and unsure, so talking after the exam would matter.

grounding: Shows a teen who craves closeness then cuts a friend off, linked to early loss, and who is supported by a counsellor to try another way.
